1: ---
2: stage: none
3: group: unassigned
4: info: For assistance with this Style Guide page, see <https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments-to-other-projects-and-subjects>.
5: description: Writing styles, markup, formatting, and other standards for the GitLab RESTful APIs.
6: title: Documenting REST API resources
7: ---
8: 
9: REST API resources are documented in Markdown under
10: [`/doc/api`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/master/doc/api). Each
11: resource has its own Markdown file, which is linked from
12: [`api_resources.md`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/master/doc/api/api_resources.md).
13: 
14: When modifying the Markdown or API code, also update the corresponding
15: [OpenAPI definition](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/master/doc/api/openapi), by running
16: `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v2:generate` and `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:generate`.
17: To check if the OpenAPI definition needs to be updated, you can run `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v2:check_docs` and
18: `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:check_docs`.
19: This is also checked by the `openapi-doc-check` CI/CD job that runs for commits that modify API code or documentation.
20: 
21: The Markdown topic for an API resource must include:
22: 
23: - A block that includes the HTTP method (like GET, PUT, DELETE) followed by the request path. Always start the path with a `/`. For example:
24: 
25:   ```plaintext
26:   GET /api/v4/projects/:id/repository/branches
27:   ```
28: 
29: - A detailed [description of the attributes](#request-attributes).
30: - A detailed [description of the response body](#response-attributes).
31: - A cURL example.
32: - A response body example (in JSON format).
33: 
34: After a new API documentation page is added, [add an entry in the global navigation](site_architecture/global_nav.md#add-a-navigation-entry).
35: 
36: ## Page metadata
37: 
38: When you create a new page, include a `description` metadata field
39: in the front matter that follows these guidelines for consistency:
40: 
41: - Start with "REST API to"
42: - Use action verbs that describe what users can do with the API
43: - Avoid words ending in -ing
44: - Keep to one sentence, ideally under 100 characters
45: - End with a period
46: 
47: For example:
48: 
49: ```yaml
50: ---
51: stage: Example Stage
52: group: Example Group
53: info: To determine the technical writer assigned to the Stage/Group associated with this page, see <https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments>
54: description: REST API to create, update, and delete issues.
55: title: Example page title
56: ---
57: ```
58: 
59: Additional examples:
60: 
61: - `description: REST API to retrieve CI/CD job details, retry and cancel jobs, run manual jobs, and access job logs.`
62: - `description: REST API to create, manage, and monitor CI/CD pipelines.`
63: 
64: ## API topic template
65: 
66: Use the following template to help you get started. Be sure to list any
67: required attributes first in the table.
68: 
69: ````markdown
70: ## API name
71: 
72: {{</* history */>}}
73: 
74: - History note.
75: 
76: {{</* /history */>}}
77: 
78: Use this API to ...
79: 
80: ### Operation title
81: 
82: {{</* history */>}}
83: 
84: - History note.
85: 
86: {{</* /history */>}}
87: 
88: Description of the operation.
89: 
90: ```plaintext
91: METHOD /api/v4/endpoint
92: ```
93: 
94: Supported attributes:
95: 
96: | Attribute                | Type     | Required | Description           |
97: |--------------------------|----------|----------|-----------------------|
98: | `attribute`              | datatype | Yes      | Detailed description. |
99: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
100: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
101: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
102: 
103: If successful, returns [`<status_code>`](rest/troubleshooting.md#status-codes) and the following
104: response attributes:
105: 
106: | Attribute                | Type     | Description           |
107: |--------------------------|----------|-----------------------|
108: | `attribute`              | datatype | Detailed description. |
109: | `attribute`              | datatype | Detailed description. |
110: 
111: Example request:
112: 
113: ```shell
114: curl --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
115:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/endpoint?parameters"
116: ```
117: 
118: Example response:
119: 
120: ```json
121: [
122:   {
123:   }
124: ]
125: ```
126: ````
127: 
128: ## History
129: 
130: Add [history](styleguide/availability_details.md#history)
131: to describe new or updated API calls.
132: 
133: To add history for an individual attribute, include it in the history
134: for the section. For example:
135: 
136: ```markdown
137: ### Edit a widget
138: 
139: {{</* history */>}}
140: 
141:  - `widget_message` [introduced](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.3.
142: 
143: {{</* /history */>}}
144: ```
145: 
146: If the API or attribute is deployed behind a feature flag,
147: [include the feature flag information](feature_flags.md) in the history.
148: 
149: ## Deprecations
150: 
151: To document the deprecation of an API endpoint, follow the steps to
152: [deprecate a page or topic](styleguide/deprecations_and_removals.md).
153: 
154: To deprecate an attribute:
155: 
156: 1. Add a history note.
157: 
158:    ```markdown
159:    {{</* history */>}}
160: 
161:    - `widget_name` [deprecated](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.7.
162: 
163:    {{</* /history */>}}
164:    ```
165: 
166: 1. Add inline deprecation text to the description.
167: 
168:    ```markdown
169:    | Attribute     | Type   | Required | Description |
170:    |---------------|--------|----------|-------------|
171:    | `widget_name` | string | No       | [Deprecated](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.7. Use `widget_id` instead. The name of the widget. |
172:    ```
173: 
174: To widely announce a deprecation, [update the REST API deprecations page](../../api/rest/deprecations.md).
175: 
176: ## API introduction
177: 
178: Each API is made of one or more operations. At the start of the topic, include information that
179: applies to all operations in the API, and a short description of the related features.
180: 
181: For consistency, try to start the introduction with: `Use this API to {verb} + [{feature}](link/to/UI/docs).`
182: This allows us to direct users to related documentation that might include more context.
183: 
184: For example:
185: 
186: - `Use this API to manage [Git branches](path/to/file).`
187: - `Use this API to interact with the [Maven package manager client](path/to/file).`
188: - `Use this API to interact with namespaces, a special resource category used to organize users and groups. For more information, see [namespaces](path/to/file).`
189: 
190: ## Operation titles
191: 
192: Start an operation title with a verb. For consistency,
193: use these verbs based on the HTTP method:
194: 
195: | HTTP method      | Verb     | Alternatives | Examples |
196: | ---------------- | -------- | ------------ | -------- |
197: | `GET` (multiple) | List all |              | `List all group access tokens` |
198: | `GET` (single)   | Retrieve | Download     | `Retrieve a group audit event`, `Download a dependency list export` |
199: | `POST`           | Create   | Add          | `Create a repository branch`, `Add a new emoji reaction` |
200: | `PUT`            | Update   | Replace      | `Update a project topic` |
201: | `PATCH`          | Update   | Modify       | `Update a freeze period`, `Modify an existing commit thread note` |
202: | `DELETE`         | Delete   |              | `Delete a feature` |
203: 
204: When possible, use the recommended verb. Alternatives might be needed in specific contexts, but
205: minimize their use to maintain consistency.
206: 
207: ## Operation descriptions
208: 
209: Each operation should include a short description that explains its use, and highlights any
210: important information. If possible, write the first sentence to broadly repeat the title of
211: the operation. For example:
212: 
213: - `List all project access tokens` -> `Lists all project access tokens.`
214: - `Delete an SSH key` -> `Deletes an SSH key from your user account.`
215: - `Retrieve an enterprise user` -> `Retrieves details on a specified enterprise user.`
216: 
217: ## Request attributes
218: 
219: You must document the request attributes in an operation. When creating the table and attribute descriptions:
220: 
221: - Use the following column names for attribute tables.
222: - List any path attributes first, then any required attributes, then sort alphabetically.
223: - Place the attribute name in code blocks using backticks (`` ` ``).
224: - Document any tier or offering information specific to an attribute in the description.
225:   - If an attribute is available for Premium, mention that it's also available for Ultimate.
226:   - Combine this tier and offering information when possible. For example: `GitLab Self-Managed, Premium and Ultimate only.`
227: 
228: ```markdown
229: | Attribute                    | Type          | Required | Description                                         |
230: |------------------------------|---------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------|
231: | `title`                      | string        | Yes      | Title of the issue. GitLab Self-Managed only.       |
232: | `assignee_ids`               | integer array | No       | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Ultimate only. |
233: | `confidential`               | boolean       | No       | Sets the issue to confidential. Default is `false`. |
234: ```
235: 
236: Rendered example:
237: 
238: | Attribute                    | Type          | Required | Description                                         |
239: |------------------------------|---------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------|
240: | `title`                      | string        | Yes      | Title of the issue. GitLab Self-Managed only.       |
241: | `assignee_ids`               | integer array | No       | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Ultimate only. |
242: | `confidential`               | boolean       | No       | Sets the issue to confidential. Default is `false`. |
243: 
244: For information about writing attribute descriptions, see the [GraphQL API description style guide](../api_graphql_styleguide.md#description-style-guide).
245: 
246: ### Conditionally required attributes
247: 
248: If an attribute is related to another item, indicate this in the attribute description.
249: 
250: Generally, this happens if one of two attributes is required or if an attribute must be enabled and configured separately.
251: 
252: First define the attribute itself, then mention any requirements. Use this format:
253: 
254:   ```markdown
255:   Required if `attribute1` is `true`.
256:   ```
257: 
258: For example:
259: 
260: | Attribute                  | Type    | Required    | Description |
261: | -------------------------- | ------- | ----------- | ----------- |
262: | `include_saml_users`       | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, returns users with a SAML identity. Required if `include_service_accounts` is `false`. |
263: | `include_service_accounts` | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, returns service account users. Required if `include_saml_users` is `false`. |
264: | `a_related_setting`        | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, does something else. Required if `include_saml_users` is `true`. |
265: 
266: ## Response attributes
267: 
268: You might sometimes need to document the response attributes in an operation. This is not usually required.
269: When creating the table and attribute descriptions:
270: 
271: - Use the following column names for attribute tables.
272: - Sort the table alphabetically.
273: - Place the attribute name in code blocks using backticks (`` ` ``).
274: - If describing an object or array, use dot notation to represent the sub-attributes. For example, `project.name` or `projects[].name`.
275: - Document any tier or offering information specific to an attribute in the description.
276:   - If an attribute is available for Premium, mention that it's also available for Ultimate.
277:   - Combine this tier and offering information when possible. For example: `GitLab Self-Managed, Premium and Ultimate only.`
278: 
279: Start the description with the following sentence, replacing `status code` with the
280: relevant [HTTP status code](../../api/rest/troubleshooting.md#status-codes), for example:
281: 
282: ```markdown
283: If successful, returns [`200 OK`](../../api/rest/troubleshooting.md#status-codes) and the
284: following response attributes:
285: ```
286: 
287: ```markdown
288: | Attribute      | Type          | Description |
289: | -------------- | ------------- | ----------- |
290: | `assignee_ids` | integer array | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Premium and Ultimate only. |
291: | `commits`      | object array  | Commits in the merge request diff. |
292: | `commits[].id` | string        | ID of the commit. |
293: ```
294: 
295: Rendered example:
296: 
297: | Attribute      | Type          | Description |
298: | -------------- | ------------- | ----------- |
299: | `assignee_ids` | integer array | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Premium and Ultimate only. |
300: | `commits`      | object array  | Commits in the merge request diff. |
301: | `commits[].id` | string        | ID of the commit. |
302: 
303: For information about writing attribute descriptions, see the [GraphQL API description style guide](../api_graphql_styleguide.md#description-style-guide).
304: 
305: ## cURL commands
306: 
307: - Use `https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/` as an endpoint.
308: - Wherever needed use this personal access token: `<your_access_token>`.
309: - Always put the request first. `GET` is the default so you don't have to
310:   include it.
311: - Use long option names (`--header` instead of `-H`) for legibility. (Tested in
312:   [`scripts/lint-doc.sh`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/master/scripts/lint-doc.sh).)
313: - Declare URLs with the `--url` parameter, and wrap the URL in double quotes (`"`).
314: - Prefer to use examples using the personal access token and don't pass data of
315:   username and password.
316: - For legibility, use the ` \ ` character and indentation to break long single-line
317:   commands apart into multiple lines.
318: 
319: | Methods                                         | Description                                            |
320: |-------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
321: | `--header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>"` | Use this method as is, whenever authentication needed. |
322: | `--request POST`                                | Use this method when creating new objects.             |
323: | `--request PUT`                                 | Use this method when updating existing objects.        |
324: | `--request DELETE`                              | Use this method when removing existing objects.        |
325: 
326: ## cURL Examples
327: 
328: The following sections include a set of [cURL](https://curl.se/) examples
329: you can use in the API documentation.
330: 
331: > [!warning]
332: > Do not use information for real users, URLs, or tokens. For documentation, refer to our
333: > relevant style guide sections on [fake user information](styleguide/_index.md#fake-user-information),
334: > [fake URLs](styleguide/_index.md#fake-urls), and [fake tokens](styleguide/_index.md#fake-tokens).
335: 
336: ### Simple cURL command
337: 
338: Get the details of a group:
339: 
340: ```shell
341: curl --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
342:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups/gitlab-org"
343: ```
344: 
345: ### cURL example with parameters passed in the URL
346: 
347: Create a new project under the authenticated user's namespace:
348: 
349: ```shell
350: curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
351:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects?name=foo"
352: ```
353: 
354: ### Post data using cURL's `--data`
355: 
356: Instead of using `--request POST` and appending the parameters to the URI, you
357: can use cURL's `--data` option. The example below creates a new project
358: `foo` under the authenticated user's namespace.
359: 
360: ```shell
361: curl --data "name=foo" \
362:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
363:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects"
364: ```
365: 
366: ### Post data using cURL's `--data-urlencode`
367: 
368: Use `--data-urlencode` when the data contains special characters that require URL encoding.
369: 
370: You can use this option for:
371: 
372: - Markdown content with code blocks or special formatting.
373: - Regular expressions containing `+`, `.`, or `*`.
374: - Text with quotes, ampersands, or other reserved URL characters.
375: - File content that might contain special characters.
376: 
377: For alphanumeric data without special characters, use [`--data`](#post-data-using-curls---data) instead.
378: 
379: For an attribute with special characters:
380: 
381: ```shell
382: curl --request POST \
383:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
384:   --data-urlencode "description=Fix issue with 'quotes' & ampersands" \
385:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/1/issues"
386: ```
387: 
388: For content with regular expression patterns:
389: 
390: ```shell
391: curl --request DELETE \
392:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
393:   --data-urlencode "name_regex_delete=dev-.+" \
394:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/5/registry/repositories/2/tags"
395: ```
396: 
397: For content from a file, use `attribute@filename`:
398: 
399: ```shell
400: curl --request POST \
401:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
402:   --data-urlencode "title=API documentation update" \
403:   --data-urlencode "content@content.md" \
404:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/1/wikis"
405: ```
406: 
407: ### Post data using JSON content
408: 
409: This example creates a new group. Be aware of the use of single (`'`) and double
410: (`"`) quotes.
411: 
412: ```shell
413: curl --request POST \
414:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
415:   --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
416:   --data '{"path": "my-group", "name": "My group"}' \
417:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups"
418: ```
419: 
420: For readability, you can also set up the `--data` by using the following format:
421: 
422: ```shell
423: curl --request POST \
424:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups" \
425:   --header "content-type: application/json" \
426:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
427:   --data '{
428:     "path": "my-group",
429:     "name": "My group"
430: }'
431: ```
432: 
433: ### Post data using form-data
434: 
435: Instead of using JSON or URL-encoding data, you can use `multipart/form-data` which
436: properly handles data encoding:
437: 
438: ```shell
439: curl --request POST \
440:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
441:   --form "title=ssh-key" \
442:   --form "key=ssh-rsa AAAAB3NzaC1yc2EA..." \
443:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/users/25/keys"
444: ```
445: 
446: The above example adds an SSH public key titled `ssh-key` to the account of
447: a user with ID 25. The operation requires administrator access.
448: 
449: ### Escape special characters
450: 
451: Spaces or slashes (`/`) can sometimes result in errors, so you should
452: escape them when possible. In the example below we create a new issue which
453: contains spaces in its title. Observe how spaces are escaped using the `%20`
454: ASCII code.
455: 
456: ```shell
457: curl --request POST \
458:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
459:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/42/issues?title=Hello%20GitLab"
460: ```
461: 
462: Use `%2F` for slashes (`/`).
463: 
464: ### Pass arrays to API calls

[{"type": "text"}, {"id": "e069a63f-1ba8-4add-9b94-e4f190ec2689", "name": "write", "arguments": "{\"filePath\":\"/work/output/taskflow_api_style_guide.md\",\"content\":\"# TaskFlow API Documentation Style Guide\\n\\n**Version:** 1.0\\n**Applies to:** All TaskFlow REST API documentation (v2 and later)\\n**Maintained by:** Technical Writing, Developer Experience\\n**Based on:** The TaskFlow RESTAPIDocs endpoint template, the per-endpoint documentation audit rubric, the OpenAPI 3.0 extract for the platform API, and the REST API documentation conventions used by mature open-source projects such as GitLab.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 1. Purpose and scope\\n\\nThis guide governs how TaskFlow writes, structures, and maintains REST API documentation. It applies to every Markdown topic published under the TaskFlow API documentation set: endpoint references, authentication guides, webhook catalogs, migration guides, and any future API version. Its goal is to make every endpoint page predictable: a developer who has read one TaskFlow endpoint should be able to read any other one without relearning the layout, the vocabulary, or the tone.\\n\\nTwo truths drive the rules below. First, our documentation has historically been written ad hoc by multiple engineers, and the audit trail shows the costs: inconsistent terminology, missing authentication notes, empty error tables, and endpoints that exist in the codebase but not on the page. Second, we maintain an OpenAPI 3.0 specification extracted from the codebase, and that specification is machine-checkable in a way prose is not. The specification therefore anchors the facts; the prose adds the judgment, context, and examples that a schema cannot carry.\\n\\n## 2. Source-of-truth hierarchy\\n\\nWhen sources disagree, resolve them in this order and record the decision in the discrepancy report:\\n\\n1. **The OpenAPI specification.** For anything a machine can verify \u2014 paths, methods, parameter names, parameter types, enums, defaults, maximums, required flags, declared response codes \u2014 the spec wins. Example: the spec enforces `maxLength: 200` on task titles, so any document that says \\\"max 255 characters\\\" is wrong regardless of how long it has said so.\\n2. **The current endpoint documentation.** For behavioral statements the spec does not express \u2014 sort order, cascade behavior descriptions, Markdown support in a field, permission rules \u2014 the documentation is the source of truth *unless* it is contradicted by the spec or flagged in the audit tracker. If we keep a documentation-only claim, we file a ticket to backfill it into the spec.\\n3. **The audit tracker.** The tracker records findings a mechanical diff cannot see: description quality, terminology drift, missing authentication notes, and stale sections. Any endpoint marked `needs_rewrite` is rewritten in full, not patched. Any endpoint marked `needs_update` must resolve every note in its row.\\n4. **Production evidence.** For behavior observable only at runtime \u2014 webhook retry counts, observed event types \u2014 the production delivery log is admissible evidence. Document observed behavior and mark it as observed, then reconcile it with the declared spec.\\n\\nNever silently reconcile. Every disagreement between sources gets a row in the discrepancy report with a resolution, even when the resolution is \\\"docs are right, spec must change.\\\"\\n\\n## 3. Page structure\\n\\nEvery endpoint reference follows the structure of the RESTAPIDocs template, extended with the conventions below. A complete operation entry contains, in this order:\\n\\n1. **Operation title** (see \u00a74).\\n2. **Method and path block** \u2014 the HTTP method followed by the full path, in a fenced `plaintext` block, with the path starting with `/`:\\n\\n   ```plaintext\\n   DELETE /api/v2/projects/{projectId}\\n   ```\\n\\n3. **Description** (see \u00a75).\\n4. **Metadata line set** from the template: `URL`, `Method`, `Auth required`, `Permissions required`.\\n5. **Request attributes table** (see \u00a76).\\n6. **Example request** (see \u00a77).\\n7. **Success response** \u2014 the status code, a response attributes table when the body has structure, and one or more example response bodies (see \u00a78).\\n8. **Error responses table** (see \u00a79).\\n9. **Notes** \u2014 anything a developer must know that does not fit above: defaults with caveats, deprecation warnings, retry behavior, rate-limit implications.\\n\\nResource-level introductions (for example, the Tasks chapter) start with one sentence in this pattern: **\\\"Use this API to {verb} {feature}.\\\"** This mirrors the introductions used by GitLab's REST API docs and gives readers an immediate purpose statement before the operations begin.\\n\\n## 4. Operation titles\\n\\nStart every operation title with a verb. Use the verb that matches the HTTP method, per the GitLab convention table, and use the same verb in the title and the first sentence of the description:\\n\\n| HTTP method | Title verb | Example title |\\n|-------------|-----------|---------------|\\n| `GET` (collection) | List all | `List all tasks` |\\n| `GET` (single item) | Retrieve | `Retrieve a task` |\\n| `POST` | Create | `Create a task` |\\n| `PUT` | Update | `Update a task` |\\n| `DELETE` | Delete | `Delete a task` |\\n\\nDo not mix verbs across a page: an endpoint titled \\\"Update a task\\\" must not describe itself as \\\"modifying\\\" the task in the body, and a project section must not drift from \\\"create\\\" to \\\"add\\\" to \\\"register\\\" mid-paragraph. The audit tracker flagged this exact drift repeatedly; it is the single most common quality defect in our legacy docs.\\n\\n## 5. Descriptions\\n\\nWrite a short description for every operation. The first sentence broadly restates the title, in the present tense, third person:\\n\\n- Title: `List all tasks` \u2192 \\\"Lists all tasks the authenticated user can access.\\\"\\n- Title: `Delete a task` \u2192 \\\"Deletes a task permanently.\\\"\\n\\nAfter the first sentence, add only what changes a developer's implementation: permission requirements, defaults, side effects (such as cascade deletion), partial-update semantics, and rate-limit implications. Do not narrate the obvious (\\\"this endpoint takes an ID and returns a task\\\"). Do not promise roadmap behavior in operative sentences; if a change is planned (for example, Unix-to-ISO 8601 migration), state it once in a Note with the target version.\\n\\n## 6. Attribute tables\\n\\nDocument every parameter and every structured response field in a Markdown table. Never describe parameters in loose bullets in a reference page; bullets are permitted in conceptual guides only.\\n\\n**Request attribute tables** use these columns: `Attribute`, `Type`, `Required`, `Description`.\\n\\n- Place path attributes first, then required attributes, then the remaining attributes alphabetically.\\n- Put every attribute name in backticks.\\n- State enums inline with backticked values: One of `open`, `in_progress`, `done`, `archived`, `blocked`.\\n- State defaults explicitly: \\\"Default is `25`.\\\"\\n- State maximums explicitly: \\\"Maximum is `200`.\\\"\\n- For conditionally required attributes, use `Conditional` in the Required column and name the condition: \\\"Required if `include_service_accounts` is `false`.\\\"\\n- Use the parameter names from the OpenAPI specification exactly. If the spec says `taskId`, the docs say `taskId` \u2014 never `task_id`, `id`, or \\\"task ID\\\" in a parameter context.\\n\\n**Response attribute tables** use these columns: `Attribute`, `Type`, `Description`, sorted alphabetically. For nested fields use dot notation: `meta.current_page`, `data[].assignee_id`.\\n\\n## 7. Request examples\\n\\nEvery operation ships at least one request example. Use cURL as the canonical example language; supplement \u2014 never replace \u2014 with a language-specific example (such as Python) only when the endpoint has unusual semantics worth demonstrating in a richer client.\\n\\ncURL conventions, adapted from GitLab's guidelines:\\n\\n- Use the production host with a placeholder token: `https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/...` and `Authorization: Bearer <your_access_token>`.\\n- Use long option names: `--header`, `--request`, `--data`, `--url`.\\n- Put the URL in `--url`, wrapped in double quotes.\\n- `GET` is implied; write `--request POST`, `--request PUT`, `--request DELETE` for everything else.\\n- Break long commands with a trailing backslash and two-space indentation.\\n- For JSON bodies, include `--header \\\"Content-Type: application/json\\\"` and pass the body in single quotes so double-quoted JSON keys survive.\\n- Use `--data-urlencode` when a value contains spaces, ampersands, or other reserved characters, and URL-encode reserved characters inside URLs (`%20` for spaces).\\n- Never use real user data, real tokens, or real customer URLs in examples.\\n\\n## 8. Response examples\\n\\nEvery operation ships at least one example response body, even when the body is empty \u2014 in that case state it: \\\"The response body is empty.\\\" Show the actual envelope shape. TaskFlow list responses use a `data` array plus a `meta` object; single-resource responses return the resource object directly (with the documented exception of `GET /users/me`, which wraps the payload in a `user` object). When multiple realistically different responses exist (for example, a user with and without optional profile data), show more than one example, as the RESTAPIDocs template does.\\n\\nIf an operation returns a non-obvious status code or empty body, say why in a Note. For every documented success response, enumerate the body fields in a response attributes table when the body is structured.\\n\\n## 9. Status codes and errors\\n\\nEvery operation documents its error responses in a two-column table: `Status code` and `Meaning`. Include at minimum the codes the OpenAPI spec declares for the operation, plus `401 Unauthorized` when the operation requires authentication. Describe the failure from the developer's perspective (\\\"Task not found, or you do not have access to it\\\") rather than from the server's.\\n\\nTaskFlow's canonical error body is:\\n\\n```json\\n{\\n  \\\"error\\\": {\\n    \\\"code\\\": \\\"VALIDATION_ERROR\\\",\\n    \\\"message\\\": \\\"Title is required\\\",\\n    \\\"details\\\": []\\n  }\\n}\\n```\\n\\nA small set of legacy endpoints still returns the flat shape `{\\\"error\\\": \\\"not_found\\\", \\\"message\\\": \\\"...\\\"}`. Documents must identify those endpoints and mark the flat shape as deprecated. Never present both shapes as equally valid; present the canonical envelope first and the legacy shape only as a marked exception.\\n\\n## 10. Cross-cutting conventions\\n\\n**Authentication.** State `Auth required: YES` or `NO` in the metadata block for every operation. Open endpoints (currently `POST /auth/login`) are listed in their own section, as the RESTAPIDocs template does. Never write \\\"all API calls require authentication\\\" in a guide if any open endpoint exists.\\n\\n**Permissions.** Where authorization is finer-grained than authentication (for example, deleting a task requires admin or owner rights on the project, or members may delete only tasks they created), document the rule in the `Permissions required` line and elaborate in Notes.\\n\\n**Pagination.** Paginated list endpoints accept `page` and `per_page`, and return pagination facts in `meta`. If an endpoint does not yet support pagination but the spec declares `page` and `per_page`, the spec is followed; if neither supports it, say so explicitly rather than leaving the reader to guess.\\n\\n**Rate limiting.** Every reference set carries one global rate-limit section stating the limits per plan, the `429 Too Many Requests` response, and the `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header. Endpoint pages link to it when rate limits materially affect the operation.\\n\\n**Timestamps.** ISO 8601 with a UTC offset (`2024-03-01T14:22:00Z`) is the documentation standard for all date-time values. Known Unix-timestamp holdovers (`projects.created`, `users.last_login`) must be called out inline as legacy fields with a note that they migrate to ISO 8601 in API v3.\\n\\n**Webhooks.** Webhook reference pages must document: the full declared event type list, the payload verification secret (HMAC), delivery retry behavior, and a link to the webhook event catalog. Use the term **webhook URL** for the destination field; do not alternate with \\\"callback URL\\\" or \\\"destination.\\\" Event names are lowercase dotted identifiers (`task.created`) and appear in backticks.\\n\\n## 11. Terminology and voice\\n\\nUse one term for one concept, everywhere:\\n\\n| Use | Do not use |\\n|-----|------------|\\n| endpoint | route, URL (when referring to the API surface) |\\n| retrieve (single item), list (collection) | fetch, get, show |\\n| parameter | argument, arg, field (for request inputs) |\\n| request body | payload |\\n| access token | JWT (in prose) |\\n| refresh the access token | rotate the token |\\n| assignee | user (when naming the assignee specifically) |\\n| delete | remove (for DELETE operations) |\\n| query parameter | query arg, filter (when naming parameters) |\\n\\nWrite in the second person (\\\"you can filter results\\\"), active voice, present tense. Avoid first person except in Notes that explicitly speak for the TaskFlow team. Avoid hedging (\\\"might possibly\\\", \\\"should generally\\\") \u2014 verify the behavior and state it.\\n\\n## 12. History, deprecation, and change management\\n\\nWhen an attribute or operation is deprecated, do three things: add a history note at the top of the section naming the version and replacement; mark the attribute inline in its table row (\\\"Deprecated in v2.1. 13: Authorization: Bearer <your_api_key>
14: ```
15: 
16: You can generate an API key from the TaskFlow dashboard under Settings > API Keys.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## Tasks
21: 
22: ### GET /api/v2/tasks
23: 
24: Retrieves a list of tasks for the authenticated user. The user can filter results using query parameters.
25: 
26: **Query Parameters**
27: 
28: | Parameter | Type | Description |
29: |-----------|------|-------------|
30: | status | string | Filter by task status. Allowed values: `open`, `in_progress`, `done`, `archived` |
31: | project_id | integer | Only return tasks belonging to this project |
32: | page | integer | Page number for pagination (default: 1) |
33: | per_page | integer | Number of results per page (default: 20, max: 100) |
34: | sort | string | Sort field. One of `created_at`, `updated_at`, `priority` |
35: | order | string | Sort direction: `asc` or `desc` |
36: 
37: **Example Request**
38: 
39: ```bash
40: curl -X GET "https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/tasks?status=open&page=1" \
41:   -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY"
42: ```
43: 
44: **Response** (200 OK)
45: 
46: ```json
47: {
48:   "data": [
49:     {
50:       "id": 1042,
51:       "title": "Fix login bug",
52:       "description": "Users are unable to login with SSO",
53:       "status": "open",
54:       "priority": "high",
55:       "assignee_id": 57,
56:       "project_id": 12,
57:       "created_at": "2024-03-01T14:22:00Z",
58:       "updated_at": "2024-03-01T14:22:00Z",
59:       "due_date": "2024-03-15T00:00:00Z"
60:     }
61:   ],
62:   "meta": {
63:     "current_page": 1,
64:     "total_pages": 5,
65:     "total_count": 98
66:   }
67: }
68: ```
69: 
70: ---
71: 
72: ### POST /api/v2/tasks
73: 
74: Creates a new task. You must provide at least a title. The task will be created under the user's default project if `project_id` is not specified.
75: 
76: **Request Body Arguments**
77: 
78: - `title` (string, **required**) - The title of the task. Max 255 characters.
79: - `description` (string) - A longer description. Supports Markdown formatting.
80: - `status` (string) - Initial status. Defaults to `open`.
81: - `priority` (string) - One of: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `critical`. Default is `medium`.
82: - `assignee_id` (integer) - User ID to assign the task to.
83: - `project_id` (integer) - Project to create the task in.
84: - `due_date` (string) - Due date in ISO 8601 format.
85: - `tags` (array of strings) - Tags to apply to the task.
86: 
87: **Example**
88: 
89: ```python
90: import requests
91: 
92: resp = requests.post(
93:     "https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/tasks",
94:     headers={"Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY"},
95:     json={
96:         "title": "Design new landing page",
97:         "description": "Create mockups for the Q2 marketing campaign",
98:         "priority": "high",
99:         "project_id": 12,
100:         "due_date": "2024-04-01T00:00:00Z",
101:         "tags": ["design", "marketing"]
102:     }
103: )
104: print(resp.json())
105: ```
106: 
107: Returns `201 Created` on success with the full task object in the response body.
108: 
109: **Errors**
110: 
111: | Status Code | Meaning |
112: |------------|---------|
113: | 400 | Bad request - missing required fields or invalid values |
114: | 401 | Authentication failed |
115: | 422 | Validation error (e.g. title too long) |
116: 
117: ---
118: 
119: ### GET /api/v2/tasks/{id}
120: 
121: Get a single task by its ID.
122: 
123: Pass the task ID as a path parameter. Returns the task object if found. Returns 404 if the task doesn't exist or you don't have access.
124: 
125: Response includes the full task object (same schema as list endpoint).
126: 
127: No additional arguments.
128: 
129: ---
130: 
131: ### Updating a task - PUT /api/v2/tasks/{id}
132: 
133: We support partial updates - you only need to send the fields you want to change. Any fields not included in the request body will remain unchanged.
134: 
135: Note: the `id` and `created_at` fields cannot be modified.
136: 
137: **Fields you can update:**
138: 
139: - title
140: - description
141: - status (must be a valid status string)
142: - priority
143: - assignee_id (set to `null` to unassign)
144: - project_id
145: - due_date (ISO 8601 timestamp or null to clear)
146: - tags
147: 
148: **Sample curl command:**
149: 
150: ```bash
151: curl -X PUT "https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/tasks/1042" \
152:   -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
153:   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
154:   -d '{"status": "in_progress", "assignee_id": 57}'
155: ```
156: 
157: The API returns `200 OK` and the updated task object on success.
158: 
159: ---
160: 
161: ### DELETE /api/v2/tasks/{id}
162: 
163: Permanently deletes a task. This action cannot be undone.
164: 
165: The user must have admin or owner permissions on the project that the task belongs to. Regular members can only delete tasks they created.
166: 
167: **Returns:**
168: 
169: `204 No Content` on success. The response body is empty.
170: 
171: If the task is not found a `404` error is returned. Attempting to delete a task without sufficient permissions results in `403 Forbidden`.
172: 
173: ---
174: 
175: ## Projects
176: 
177: ### List projects
178: 
179: ```
180: GET /api/v2/projects
181: ```
182: 
183: This route returns all projects the authenticated user has access to. Projects are returned in alphabetical order by name.
184: 
185: **Query args:**
186: 
187: - `archived` (boolean) - if `true`, include archived projects. Default `false`.
188: - `role` (string) - filter by the user's role in the project: `owner`, `admin`, `member`
189: 
190: No authentication header examples are given here since it follows the same pattern described at the top of this doc.
191: 
192: **Sample response:**
193: 
194: ```json
195: {
196:   "projects": [
197:     {
198:       "id": 12,
199:       "name": "Website Redesign",
200:       "description": "Q2 2024 website overhaul",
201:       "owner_id": 57,
202:       "created": 1709312400,
203:       "member_count": 8,
204:       "task_count": 45,
205:       "archived": false
206:     }
207:   ]
208: }
209: ```
210: 
211: Note that the `created` field here returns a Unix timestamp. We plan to migrate this to ISO 8601 in a future release.
212: 
213: ---
214: 
215: ### Create Project
216: 
217: **Endpoint:** `POST /api/v2/projects`
218: 
219: To create a new project, send a POST request with the following payload:
220: 
221: ```json
222: {
223:   "name": "My New Project",
224:   "description": "Optional project description"
225: }
226: ```
227: 
228: The `name` field is required and must be unique within the user's organization. Max 100 chars.
229: 
230: **Response fields:**
231: 
232: | Field | Type | Notes |
233: |-------|------|-------|
234: | id | integer | Auto-generated project ID |
235: | name | string | The project name |
236: | description | string | May be null |
237: | owner_id | integer | ID of creating user |
238: | created | integer | Unix timestamp |
239: | member_count | integer | Always 1 for new projects |
240: | task_count | integer | Always 0 for new projects |
241: | archived | boolean | Always false for new projects |
242: 
243: Returns HTTP 201.
244: 
245: No error documentation is provided here but the API follows standard REST conventions for error responses.
246: 
247: ---
248: 
249: ## User Info
250: 
251: ### Getting your profile
252: 
253: **Route**: GET /api/v2/users/me
254: 
255: This returns information about the currently authenticated user. Pass your API key as usual.
256: 
257: The response looks like:
258: 
259: ```json
260: {
261:   "user": {
262:     "id": 57,
263:     "email": "jane@example.com",
264:     "name": "Jane Smith",
265:     "role": "admin",
266:     "organization_id": 5,
267:     "timezone": "America/New_York",
268:     "created_at": "2023-01-15T09:00:00Z",
269:     "last_login": 1709398800
270:   }
271: }
272: ```
273: 
274: Note: `created_at` is ISO 8601 but `last_login` is a Unix timestamp. This inconsistency will be addressed in API v3.
275: 
276: ---
277: 
278: ## Rate Limiting
279: 
280: We enforce rate limits to ensure fair usage of the API. The current limits are:
281: 
282: - 100 requests per minute for free tier
283: - 1000 requests per minute for paid plans
284: 
285: When you exceed the limit, the API returns `429 Too Many Requests`. Check the `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header to see how many requests you have left.
286: 
287: ## Pagination
288: 
289: List endpoints support pagination via `page` and `per_page` query parameters. The response `meta` object contains pagination info. Note that the projects endpoint does not currently support pagination - all projects are returned in a single response.
290: 
291: ## Errors
292: 
293: The API uses standard HTTP status codes. Error responses include a JSON body:
294: 
295: ```json
296: {
297:   "error": {
298:     "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
299:     "message": "Title is required",
300:     "details": []
301:   }
302: }
303: ```
304: 
305: However, some older endpoints may return errors in a different format:
306: 
307: ```json
308: {
309:   "error": "not_found",
310:   "message": "Task not found"
311: }
312: ```
313: 
314: We are working on standardizing error responses across all routes.
315: 
316: ---
317: 
318: *For questions or support, email api-support@taskflow.io*

1: # TaskFlow API v1
2: 
3: API base URL: `https://api.taskflow.io/api`
4: 
5: Auth: use `X-API-Key` header with your key.
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## GET /api/tasks
10: 
11: Gets tasks. Returns JSON array.
12: 
13: Params: `status`, `project`, `limit`, `offset`
14: 
15: Response: array of task objects.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## POST /api/tasks
20: 
21: Create a task.
22: 
23: Body: JSON with `title` (required), `desc`, `status`, `priority`, `assigned_to`, `project`, `deadline`.
24: 
25: `deadline` should be a Unix timestamp.
26: 
27: Returns the created task. 200 OK.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## GET /api/tasks/:id
32: 
33: Fetch one task.
34: 
35: ---
36: 
37: ## PUT /api/tasks/:id
38: 
39: Update task fields. Send only what changed.
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## DELETE /api/tasks/:id
44: 
45: Delete a task. Must be owner.
46: 
47: ---
48: 
49: ## GET /api/projects
50: 
51: List all projects.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ## POST /api/projects
56: 
57: Make a new project. Body: `name` (required), `desc`.
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ## GET /api/users/current
62: 
63: Get current user info.
64: 
65: Response:
66: 
67: ```
68: {
69:   "id": 57,
70:   "email": "jane@example.com",
71:   "name": "Jane Smith",
72:   "role": "admin",
73:   "org": 5
74: }
75: ```
76: 
77: ---
78: 
79: ## GET /api/tasks/:id/comments
80: 
81: List comments on a task.
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ## POST /api/tasks/:id/comments
86: 
87: Add comment. Body: `text`.
88: 
89: ---
90: 
91: ## GET /api/search
92: 
93: Search across tasks and projects.
94: 
95: Params: `q` (search query), `type` (task or project)
96: 
97: ---
98: 
99: ## PUT /api/tasks/:id/assign
100: 
101: Assign a task to a user. Body: `user_id`.
102: 
103: This is a convenience endpoint. You can also update the `assigned_to` field directly via PUT /api/tasks/:id.
104: 
105: ---
106: 
107: ## GET /api/tasks/:id/history
108: 
109: Returns change history for a task. Each entry shows what field changed, old value, new value, who changed it, and when (Unix timestamp).
110: 
111: ---
112: 
113: ## DELETE /api/projects/:id
114: 
115: Delete a project. All tasks in the project will also be deleted.
116: 
117: ---
118: 
119: ## Errors
120: 
121: Errors return JSON: `{"error": "message"}`.
122: 
123: Common codes: 400, 401, 404, 500.
124: 
125: ---
126: 
127: ## Webhooks
128: 
129: POST /api/webhooks - register a webhook. Body: `url`, `events` (array).
130: 
131: GET /api/webhooks - list webhooks.
132: 
133: DELETE /api/webhooks/:id - remove a webhook.
134: 
135: Events: `task.created`, `task.updated`, `task.deleted`, `project.created`.
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## Notes
140: 
141: - Rate limit: 60 req/min.
142: - All timestamps are Unix.
143: - Contact support@taskflow.io for help.

1: ---
2: stage: none
3: group: unassigned
4: info: For assistance with this Style Guide page, see <https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments-to-other-projects-and-subjects>.
5: description: Writing styles, markup, formatting, and other standards for the GitLab RESTful APIs.
6: title: Documenting REST API resources
7: ---
8: 
9: REST API resources are documented in Markdown under
10: [`/doc/api`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/master/doc/api). Each
11: resource has its own Markdown file, which is linked from
12: [`api_resources.md`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/master/doc/api/api_resources.md).
13: 
14: When modifying the Markdown or API code, also update the corresponding
15: [OpenAPI definition](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/master/doc/api/openapi), by running
16: `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v2:generate` and `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:generate`.
17: To check if the OpenAPI definition needs to be updated, you can run `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v2:check_docs` and
18: `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:check_docs`.
19: This is also checked by the `openapi-doc-check` CI/CD job that runs for commits that modify API code or documentation.
20: 
21: The Markdown topic for an API resource must include:
22: 
23: - A block that includes the HTTP method (like GET, PUT, DELETE) followed by the request path. Always start the path with a `/`. For example:
24: 
25:   ```plaintext
26:   GET /api/v4/projects/:id/repository/branches
27:   ```
28: 
29: - A detailed [description of the attributes](#request-attributes).
30: - A detailed [description of the response body](#response-attributes).
31: - A cURL example.
32: - A response body example (in JSON format).
33: 
34: After a new API documentation page is added, [add an entry in the global navigation](site_architecture/global_nav.md#add-a-navigation-entry).
35: 
36: ## Page metadata
37: 
38: When you create a new page, include a `description` metadata field
39: in the front matter that follows these guidelines for consistency:
40: 
41: - Start with "REST API to"
42: - Use action verbs that describe what users can do with the API
43: - Avoid words ending in -ing
44: - Keep to one sentence, ideally under 100 characters
45: - End with a period
46: 
47: For example:
48: 
49: ```yaml
50: ---
51: stage: Example Stage
52: group: Example Group
53: info: To determine the technical writer assigned to the Stage/Group associated with this page, see <https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments>
54: description: REST API to create, update, and delete issues.
55: title: Example page title
56: ---
57: ```
58: 
59: Additional examples:
60: 
61: - `description: REST API to retrieve CI/CD job details, retry and cancel jobs, run manual jobs, and access job logs.`
62: - `description: REST API to create, manage, and monitor CI/CD pipelines.`
63: 
64: ## API topic template
65: 
66: Use the following template to help you get started. Be sure to list any
67: required attributes first in the table.
68: 
69: ````markdown
70: ## API name
71: 
72: {{</* history */>}}
73: 
74: - History note.
75: 
76: {{</* /history */>}}
77: 
78: Use this API to ...
79: 
80: ### Operation title
81: 
82: {{</* history */>}}
83: 
84: - History note.
85: 
86: {{</* /history */>}}
87: 
88: Description of the operation.
89: 
90: ```plaintext
91: METHOD /api/v4/endpoint
92: ```
93: 
94: Supported attributes:
95: 
96: | Attribute                | Type     | Required | Description           |
97: |--------------------------|----------|----------|-----------------------|
98: | `attribute`              | datatype | Yes      | Detailed description. |
99: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
100: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
101: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
102: 
103: If successful, returns [`<status_code>`](rest/troubleshooting.md#status-codes) and the following
104: response attributes:
105: 
106: | Attribute                | Type     | Description           |
107: |--------------------------|----------|-----------------------|
108: | `attribute`              | datatype | Detailed description. |
109: | `attribute`              | datatype | Detailed description. |
110: 
111: Example request:
112: 
113: ```shell
114: curl --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
115:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/endpoint?parameters"
116: ```
117: 
118: Example response:
119: 
120: ```json
121: [
122:   {
123:   }
124: ]
125: ```
126: ````
127: 
128: ## History
129: 
130: Add [history](styleguide/availability_details.md#history)
131: to describe new or updated API calls.
132: 
133: To add history for an individual attribute, include it in the history
134: for the section. For example:
135: 
136: ```markdown
137: ### Edit a widget
138: 
139: {{</* history */>}}
140: 
141:  - `widget_message` [introduced](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.3.
142: 
143: {{</* /history */>}}
144: ```
145: 
146: If the API or attribute is deployed behind a feature flag,
147: [include the feature flag information](feature_flags.md) in the history.
148: 
149: ## Deprecations
150: 
151: To document the deprecation of an API endpoint, follow the steps to
152: [deprecate a page or topic](styleguide/deprecations_and_removals.md).
153: 
154: To deprecate an attribute:
155: 
156: 1. Add a history note.
157: 
158:    ```markdown
159:    {{</* history */>}}
160: 
161:    - `widget_name` [deprecated](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.7.
162: 
163:    {{</* /history */>}}
164:    ```
165: 
166: 1. Add inline deprecation text to the description.
167: 
168:    ```markdown
169:    | Attribute     | Type   | Required | Description |
170:    |---------------|--------|----------|-------------|
171:    | `widget_name` | string | No       | [Deprecated](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.7. Use `widget_id` instead. The name of the widget. |
172:    ```
173: 
174: To widely announce a deprecation, [update the REST API deprecations page](../../api/rest/deprecations.md).
175: 
176: ## API introduction
177: 
178: Each API is made of one or more operations. At the start of the topic, include information that
179: applies to all operations in the API, and a short description of the related features.
180: 
181: For consistency, try to start the introduction with: `Use this API to {verb} + [{feature}](link/to/UI/docs).`
182: This allows us to direct users to related documentation that might include more context.
183: 
184: For example:
185: 
186: - `Use this API to manage [Git branches](path/to/file).`
187: - `Use this API to interact with the [Maven package manager client](path/to/file).`
188: - `Use this API to interact with namespaces, a special resource category used to organize users and groups. For more information, see [namespaces](path/to/file).`
189: 
190: ## Operation titles
191: 
192: Start an operation title with a verb. For consistency,
193: use these verbs based on the HTTP method:
194: 
195: | HTTP method      | Verb     | Alternatives | Examples |
196: | ---------------- | -------- | ------------ | -------- |
197: | `GET` (multiple) | List all |              | `List all group access tokens` |
198: | `GET` (single)   | Retrieve | Download     | `Retrieve a group audit event`, `Download a dependency list export` |
199: | `POST`           | Create   | Add          | `Create a repository branch`, `Add a new emoji reaction` |
200: | `PUT`            | Update   | Replace      | `Update a project topic` |
201: | `PATCH`          | Update   | Modify       | `Update a freeze period`, `Modify an existing commit thread note` |
202: | `DELETE`         | Delete   |              | `Delete a feature` |
203: 
204: When possible, use the recommended verb. Alternatives might be needed in specific contexts, but
205: minimize their use to maintain consistency.
206: 
207: ## Operation descriptions
208: 
209: Each operation should include a short description that explains its use, and highlights any
210: important information. If possible, write the first sentence to broadly repeat the title of
211: the operation. For example:
212: 
213: - `List all project access tokens` -> `Lists all project access tokens.`
214: - `Delete an SSH key` -> `Deletes an SSH key from your user account.`
215: - `Retrieve an enterprise user` -> `Retrieves details on a specified enterprise user.`
216: 
217: ## Request attributes
218: 
219: You must document the request attributes in an operation. When creating the table and attribute descriptions:
220: 
221: - Use the following column names for attribute tables.
222: - List any path attributes first, then any required attributes, then sort alphabetically.
223: - Place the attribute name in code blocks using backticks (`` ` ``).
224: - Document any tier or offering information specific to an attribute in the description.
225:   - If an attribute is available for Premium, mention that it's also available for Ultimate.
226:   - Combine this tier and offering information when possible. For example: `GitLab Self-Managed, Premium and Ultimate only.`
227: 
228: ```markdown
229: | Attribute                    | Type          | Required | Description                                         |
230: |------------------------------|---------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------|
231: | `title`                      | string        | Yes      | Title of the issue. GitLab Self-Managed only.       |
232: | `assignee_ids`               | integer array | No       | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Ultimate only. |
233: | `confidential`               | boolean       | No       | Sets the issue to confidential. Default is `false`. |
234: ```
235: 
236: Rendered example:
237: 
238: | Attribute                    | Type          | Required | Description                                         |
239: |------------------------------|---------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------|
240: | `title`                      | string        | Yes      | Title of the issue. GitLab Self-Managed only.       |
241: | `assignee_ids`               | integer array | No       | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Ultimate only. |
242: | `confidential`               | boolean       | No       | Sets the issue to confidential. Default is `false`. |
243: 
244: For information about writing attribute descriptions, see the [GraphQL API description style guide](../api_graphql_styleguide.md#description-style-guide).
245: 
246: ### Conditionally required attributes
247: 
248: If an attribute is related to another item, indicate this in the attribute description.
249: 
250: Generally, this happens if one of two attributes is required or if an attribute must be enabled and configured separately.
251: 
252: First define the attribute itself, then mention any requirements. Use this format:
253: 
254:   ```markdown
255:   Required if `attribute1` is `true`.
256:   ```
257: 
258: For example:
259: 
260: | Attribute                  | Type    | Required    | Description |
261: | -------------------------- | ------- | ----------- | ----------- |
262: | `include_saml_users`       | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, returns users with a SAML identity. Required if `include_service_accounts` is `false`. |
263: | `include_service_accounts` | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, returns service account users. Required if `include_saml_users` is `false`. |
264: | `a_related_setting`        | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, does something else. Required if `include_saml_users` is `true`. |
265: 
266: ## Response attributes
267: 
268: You might sometimes need to document the response attributes in an operation. This is not usually required.
269: When creating the table and attribute descriptions:
270: 
271: - Use the following column names for attribute tables.
272: - Sort the table alphabetically.
273: - Place the attribute name in code blocks using backticks (`` ` ``).
274: - If describing an object or array, use dot notation to represent the sub-attributes. For example, `project.name` or `projects[].name`.
275: - Document any tier or offering information specific to an attribute in the description.
276:   - If an attribute is available for Premium, mention that it's also available for Ultimate.
277:   - Combine this tier and offering information when possible. For example: `GitLab Self-Managed, Premium and Ultimate only.`
278: 
279: Start the description with the following sentence, replacing `status code` with the
280: relevant [HTTP status code](../../api/rest/troubleshooting.md#status-codes), for example:
281: 
282: ```markdown
283: If successful, returns [`200 OK`](../../api/rest/troubleshooting.md#status-codes) and the
284: following response attributes:
285: ```
286: 
287: ```markdown
288: | Attribute      | Type          | Description |
289: | -------------- | ------------- | ----------- |
290: | `assignee_ids` | integer array | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Premium and Ultimate only. |
291: | `commits`      | object array  | Commits in the merge request diff. |
292: | `commits[].id` | string        | ID of the commit. |
293: ```
294: 
295: Rendered example:
296: 
297: | Attribute      | Type          | Description |
298: | -------------- | ------------- | ----------- |
299: | `assignee_ids` | integer array | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Premium and Ultimate only. |
300: | `commits`      | object array  | Commits in the merge request diff. |
301: | `commits[].id` | string        | ID of the commit. |
302: 
303: For information about writing attribute descriptions, see the [GraphQL API description style guide](../api_graphql_styleguide.md#description-style-guide).
304: 
305: ## cURL commands
306: 
307: - Use `https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/` as an endpoint.
308: - Wherever needed use this personal access token: `<your_access_token>`.
309: - Always put the request first. `GET` is the default so you don't have to
310:   include it.
311: - Use long option names (`--header` instead of `-H`) for legibility. (Tested in
312:   [`scripts/lint-doc.sh`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/master/scripts/lint-doc.sh).)
313: - Declare URLs with the `--url` parameter, and wrap the URL in double quotes (`"`).
314: - Prefer to use examples using the personal access token and don't pass data of
315:   username and password.
316: - For legibility, use the ` \ ` character and indentation to break long single-line
317:   commands apart into multiple lines.
318: 
319: | Methods                                         | Description                                            |
320: |-------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
321: | `--header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>"` | Use this method as is, whenever authentication needed. |
322: | `--request POST`                                | Use this method when creating new objects.             |
323: | `--request PUT`                                 | Use this method when updating existing objects.        |
324: | `--request DELETE`                              | Use this method when removing existing objects.        |
325: 
326: ## cURL Examples
327: 
328: The following sections include a set of [cURL](https://curl.se/) examples
329: you can use in the API documentation.
330: 
331: > [!warning]
332: > Do not use information for real users, URLs, or tokens. For documentation, refer to our
333: > relevant style guide sections on [fake user information](styleguide/_index.md#fake-user-information),
334: > [fake URLs](styleguide/_index.md#fake-urls), and [fake tokens](styleguide/_index.md#fake-tokens).
335: 
336: ### Simple cURL command
337: 
338: Get the details of a group:
339: 
340: ```shell
341: curl --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
342:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups/gitlab-org"
343: ```
344: 
345: ### cURL example with parameters passed in the URL
346: 
347: Create a new project under the authenticated user's namespace:
348: 
349: ```shell
350: curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
351:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects?name=foo"
352: ```
353: 
354: ### Post data using cURL's `--data`
355: 
356: Instead of using `--request POST` and appending the parameters to the URI, you
357: can use cURL's `--data` option. The example below creates a new project
358: `foo` under the authenticated user's namespace.
359: 
360: ```shell
361: curl --data "name=foo" \
362:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
363:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects"
364: ```
365: 
366: ### Post data using cURL's `--data-urlencode`
367: 
368: Use `--data-urlencode` when the data contains special characters that require URL encoding.
369: 
370: You can use this option for:
371: 
372: - Markdown content with code blocks or special formatting.
373: - Regular expressions containing `+`, `.`, or `*`.
374: - Text with quotes, ampersands, or other reserved URL characters.
375: - File content that might contain special characters.
376: 
377: For alphanumeric data without special characters, use [`--data`](#post-data-using-curls---data) instead.
378: 
379: For an attribute with special characters:
380: 
381: ```shell
382: curl --request POST \
383:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
384:   --data-urlencode "description=Fix issue with 'quotes' & ampersands" \
385:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/1/issues"
386: ```
387:

Purpose and scope\n\nThis guide governs how TaskFlow writes, structures, and maintains REST API documentation. It applies to every Markdown topic published under the TaskFlow API documentation set: endpoint references, authentication guides, webhook catalogs, migration guides, and any future API version. Its goal is to make every endpoint page predictable: a developer who has read one TaskFlow endpoint should be able to read any other one without relearning the layout, the vocabulary, or the tone.\n\nTwo truths drive the rules below. First, our documentation has historically been written ad hoc by multiple engineers, and the audit trail shows the costs: inconsistent terminology, missing authentication notes, empty error tables, and endpoints that exist in the codebase but not on the page. Second, we maintain an OpenAPI 3.0 specification extracted from the codebase, and that specification is machine-checkable in a way prose is not. The specification therefore anchors the facts; the prose adds the judgment, context, and examples that a schema cannot carry.\n\n## 2. Source-of-truth hierarchy\n\nWhen sources disagree, resolve them in this order and record the decision in the discrepancy report:\n\n1. **The OpenAPI specification.** For anything a machine can verify — paths, methods, parameter names, parameter types, enums, defaults, maximums, required flags, declared response codes — the spec wins. Example: the spec enforces `maxLength: 200` on task titles, so any document that says \"max 255 characters\" is wrong regardless of how long it has said so.\n2. **The current endpoint documentation.** For behavioral statements the spec does not express — sort order, cascade behavior descriptions, Markdown support in a field, permission rules — the documentation is the source of truth *unless* it is contradicted by the spec or flagged in the audit tracker. If we keep a documentation-only claim, we file a ticket to backfill it into the spec.\n3. **The audit tracker.** The tracker records findings a mechanical diff cannot see: description quality, terminology drift, missing authentication notes, and stale sections. Any endpoint marked `needs_rewrite` is rewritten in full, not patched. Any endpoint marked `needs_update` must resolve every note in its row.\n4. **Production evidence.** For behavior observable only at runtime — webhook retry counts, observed event types — the production delivery log is admissible evidence. Document observed behavior and mark it as observed, then reconcile it with the declared spec.\n\nNever silently reconcile. Every disagreement between sources gets a row in the discrepancy report with a resolution, even when the resolution is \"docs are right, spec must change.\"\n\n## 3. Page structure\n\nEvery endpoint reference follows the structure of the RESTAPIDocs template, extended with the conventions below. A complete operation entry contains, in this order:\n\n1. **Operation title** (see §4).\n2. **Method and path block** — the HTTP method followed by the full path, in a fenced `plaintext` block, with the path starting with `/`:\n\n   ```plaintext\n   DELETE /api/v2/projects/{projectId}\n   ```\n\n3. **Description** (see §5).\n4. **Metadata line set** from the template: `URL`, `Method`, `Auth required`, `Permissions required`.\n5. **Request attributes table** (see §6).\n6. **Example request** (see §7).\n7. **Success response** — the status code, a response attributes table when the body has structure, and one or more example response bodies (see §8).\n8. **Error responses table** (see §9).\n9. **Notes** — anything a developer must know that does not fit above: defaults with caveats, deprecation warnings, retry behavior, rate-limit implications.\n\nResource-level introductions (for example, the Tasks chapter) start with one sentence in this pattern: **\"Use this API to {verb} {feature}.\"** This mirrors the introductions used by GitLab's REST API docs and gives readers an immediate purpose statement before the operations begin.\n\n## 4. Operation titles\n\nStart every operation title with a verb. Use the verb that matches the HTTP method, per the GitLab convention table, and use the same verb in the title and the first sentence of the description:\n\n| HTTP method | Title verb | Example title |\n|-------------|-----------|---------------|\n| `GET` (collection) | List all | `List all tasks` |\n| `GET` (single item) | Retrieve | `Retrieve a task` |\n| `POST` | Create | `Create a task` |\n| `PUT` | Update | `Update a task` |\n| `DELETE` | Delete | `Delete a task` |\n\nDo not mix verbs across a page: an endpoint titled \"Update a task\" must not describe itself as \"modifying\" the task in the body, and a project section must not drift from \"create\" to \"add\" to \"register\" mid-paragraph. The audit tracker flagged this exact drift repeatedly; it is the single most common quality defect in our legacy docs.\n\n## 5. Descriptions\n\nWrite a short description for every operation. The first sentence broadly restates the title, in the present tense, third person:\n\n- Title: `List all tasks` → \"Lists all tasks the authenticated user can access.\"\n- Title: `Delete a task` → \"Deletes a task permanently.\"\n\nAfter the first sentence, add only what changes a developer's implementation: permission requirements, defaults, side effects (such as cascade deletion), partial-update semantics, and rate-limit implications. Do not narrate the obvious (\"this endpoint takes an ID and returns a task\"). Do not promise roadmap behavior in operative sentences; if a change is planned (for example, Unix-to-ISO 8601 migration), state it once in a Note with the target version.\n\n## 6. Attribute tables\n\nDocument every parameter and every structured response field in a Markdown table. Never describe parameters in loose bullets in a reference page; bullets are permitted in conceptual guides only.\n\n**Request attribute tables** use these columns: `Attribute`, `Type`, `Required`, `Description`.\n\n- Place path attributes first, then required attributes, then the remaining attributes alphabetically.\n- Put every attribute name in backticks.\n- State enums inline with backticked values: One of `open`, `in_progress`, `done`, `archived`, `blocked`.\n- State defaults explicitly: \"Default is `25`.\"\n- State maximums explicitly: \"Maximum is `200`.\"\n- For conditionally required attributes, use `Conditional` in the Required column and name the condition: \"Required if `include_service_accounts` is `false`.\"\n- Use the parameter names from the OpenAPI specification exactly. If the spec says `taskId`, the docs say `taskId` — never `task_id`, `id`, or \"task ID\" in a parameter context.\n\n**Response attribute tables** use these columns: `Attribute`, `Type`, `Description`, sorted alphabetically. For nested fields use dot notation: `meta.current_page`, `data[].assignee_id`.\n\n## 7. Request examples\n\nEvery operation ships at least one request example. Use cURL as the canonical example language; supplement — never replace — with a language-specific example (such as Python) only when the endpoint has unusual semantics worth demonstrating in a richer client.\n\ncURL conventions, adapted from GitLab's guidelines:\n\n- Use the production host with a placeholder token: `https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/...` and `Authorization: Bearer <your_access_token>`.\n- Use long option names: `--header`, `--request`, `--data`, `--url`.\n- Put the URL in `--url`, wrapped in double quotes.\n- `GET` is implied; write `--request POST`, `--request PUT`, `--request DELETE` for everything else.\n- Break long commands with a trailing backslash and two-space indentation.\n- For JSON bodies, include `--header \"Content-Type: application/json\"` and pass the body in single quotes so double-quoted JSON keys survive.\n- Use `--data-urlencode` when a value contains spaces, ampersands, or other reserved characters, and URL-encode reserved characters inside URLs (`%20` for spaces).\n- Never use real user data, real tokens, or real customer URLs in examples.\n\n## 8. Response examples\n\nEvery operation ships at least one example response body, even when the body is empty — in that case state it: \"The response body is empty.\" Show the actual envelope shape. TaskFlow list responses use a `data` array plus a `meta` object; single-resource responses return the resource object directly (with the documented exception of `GET /users/me`, which wraps the payload in a `user` object). When multiple realistically different responses exist (for example, a user with and without optional profile data), show more than one example, as the RESTAPIDocs template does.\n\nIf an operation returns a non-obvious status code or empty body, say why in a Note. For every documented success response, enumerate the body fields in a response attributes table when the body is structured.\n\n## 9. Status codes and errors\n\nEvery operation documents its error responses in a two-column table: `Status code` and `Meaning`. Include at minimum the codes the OpenAPI spec declares for the operation, plus `401 Unauthorized` when the operation requires authentication.
